title: Builtin or external program?
description: Sort commands by whether bash runs them itself or starts a program file from disk.

items.why: `type -a cd` prints only "cd is a shell builtin". It has to be one, since a separate program could change only its own directory, never the shell’s.
`type -a ls` shows only paths: `/usr/bin/ls` and `/bin/ls`. It is a program file found through `PATH`.
`type -a pwd` lists the shell builtin first, then `/usr/bin/pwd` and `/bin/pwd`. It exists in both forms, but bash runs the builtin.
`type -a cat` shows only `/usr/bin/cat` and `/bin/cat`. There is no builtin.
`type -a echo` lists the builtin first and then `/usr/bin/echo` and `/bin/echo`. It exists in both forms, but typing `echo` runs bash’s builtin.
`type` reports "type is a shell builtin". It has to be part of the shell, since the shell is what knows how commands are resolved.
`export` says "export is a shell builtin". It changes the shell’s own variables, which no separate program could do.
On Debian, `type -a which` shows `/usr/bin/which` and `/bin/which`. It is a separate program, so unlike `type` it does not know about builtins.
`history` is "a shell builtin": it shows the command history that the running bash keeps.
`type -a man` shows `/usr/bin/man` and `/bin/man`. It is a program that opens manual pages.
`alias` is "a shell builtin", since aliases are part of the shell’s own state.
`type -a sudo` shows `/usr/bin/sudo` and `/bin/sudo`. It is a program that starts another command with other rights.
`exit` is "a shell builtin": it ends the shell itself.
`type -a tar` shows `/usr/bin/tar` and `/bin/tar`. It is a separate program.
`read` is "a shell builtin" that reads a line into a shell variable. A separate program could not set the shell’s variables.
